[1] This program serves as a comprehensive guide for FDA personnel, including investigators, laboratory analysts, and compliance officers, detailing the agency's procedures for inspections, sample collection and analysis, and other compliance activities. [1] The update is part of a broader effort to enhance the safety and resilience of the infant formula supply in the United States, building on lessons learned from recent challenges and incorporating new requirements from the Food and Drug Omnibus Reform Act of 2022. [1, 6] Key additions to the program include instructions for annual environmental sampling for Cronobacter and Salmonella at powdered infant formula facilities and protocols for immediate notification and escalation if tests show positive results for these pathogens or nutrient levels that are outside of required ranges. [1, 3] <2> On October 5, 2023, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) issued a warning letter to Golden Natural Products for failing to establish a Foreign Supplier Verification Program (FSVP). [1, 2] An inspection of the New York import company, conducted from July 11-13, 2023, revealed that the firm was not in compliance with federal regulations because it had not developed, maintained, and followed an FSVP. [2, 5, 6] The warning specifically cited the company's failure to create a program for imported products such as dried apricots and dried cherry plums. [3, 4] <3> The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) issued its final guidance on September 28, 2023, establishing updated standards for the growing, harvesting, packing, and holding of sprouts for human consumption. Sprouts are identified as a high-risk food because the conditions ideal for their growth also facilitate the proliferation of dangerous pathogens. The comprehensive recommendations cover critical areas such as cleaning and sanitization, the use of agricultural water, seed treatment, environmental monitoring, and meticulous recordkeeping. <4> In recognition of National Food Safety Education Month in September 2023, the USDA's Food and Nutrition Service (FNS) released five new factsheets on September 18, 2023. The agency stated the products were sold illegally in the U.S. because the New Zealand-based company had not submitted the required premarket notification to demonstrate the formula's safety and nutritional adequacy. Consequently, the products were not evaluated to ensure they meet U.S. standards. The FDA noted particular concerns with the formula's preparation instructions, which do not align with U.S. measurements and could lead to improper mixing, potentially causing undernutrition or dehydration. Titled 'Facing Food Safety Challenges through Culture and Persistence,' the webinar focused on the importance of a strong food safety culture in helping organizations address challenges. The event featured guest speakers Kerry Bridges, Vice President of Food Safety at Chipotle Mexican Grill, and Al Almanza, Global Head of Food Safety and Quality Assurance at JBS Foods. Additional speakers included Lone Jespersen, Principal and Founder of Cultivate SA, and Dr. Conrad Choiniere, an office Director at the FDA's Center for Food Safety and Applied Nutrition. The series is designed to create a collaborative exchange between public and private sector experts on influencing beliefs, attitudes, and behaviors to reduce foodborne illness. <7> September 2023 was National Food Safety Education Month, an annual observance to promote practices that prevent foodborne illness. [1] The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) spearheaded the 2023 campaign with a particular focus on populations at a higher risk of serious illness, such as pregnant women, older adults, young children, and those with weakened immune systems. [1, 2, 5] An estimated 1 in 6 Americans, or 48 million people, get sick from foodborne illnesses annually, leading to about 128,000 hospitalizations and 3,000 deaths. [2, 3] To mitigate this, the FDA emphasized four key steps for safe food handling: Clean, Separate, Cook, and Chill. [1, 2] The campaign provided numerous resources for consumers and health educators to understand risks associated with foods like undercooked meats, unpasteurized dairy, and raw shellfish, and to implement safe practices at home. [1, 5, 6]

[2, 6] The recalled products were distributed nationwide under various brand names, including Tio Francisco, Don Francisco, Rizo Bros, and 365 Whole Foods Market, and were also sold at retail deli counters. [2, 7] An initial, smaller recall was issued on January 11, 2024, after the outbreak strain was found in a sample of aged cotija cheese by Hawaiian health officials. [5] The broader recall was announced on February 5, 2024, after new illnesses were reported and the FDA found the outbreak strain in the manufacturing facility. [2, 5, 3] <2> In February 2024, the FDA and USDA oversaw a significant series of food product recalls primarily due to potential contamination with *Listeria monocytogenes*. The central event was a voluntary recall by Rizo-López Foods, Inc., which began with a single batch of Cotija cheese on January 11, 2024, after the bacterium was detected by health officials in Hawaii. This escalated significantly on February 5, 2024, when the company, in cooperation with the FDA and CDC, recalled all its cheese, yogurt, and sour cream products. These dairy items were identified as a potential source of a multi-year, nationwide *Listeria* outbreak that has caused 26 illnesses, 23 hospitalizations, and two deaths since 2014. The recall impacted numerous brands, including Tio Francisco, Don Francisco, Rizo Bros, and 365 Whole Foods Market, sold at major retailers nationwide. The Rizo-López Foods recall led to a cascade of secondary recalls from other companies, like Sargento Foods, that used the contaminated dairy products as ingredients in their own food service items. Sargento initiated its recall on February 5, 2024, for products distributed in at least 15 states. The Food Industry Counsel maintains a list of these recalls, providing a searchable database of FDA and USDA recalls. <3> On January 25, 2024, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration's (FDA) Foods Program published an updated list of guidance topics it intends to address through draft or final documents by the end of 2024. This update is part of the FDA's effort to increase transparency and inform stakeholders of its regulatory priorities. Key additions to the guidance agenda include action levels for lead in baby foods, Question and Answer guidance for the Food Traceability Rule, and preventive controls for chemical hazards. Other significant topics slated for guidance include the labeling of plant-based alternatives, voluntary sodium reduction goals, and premarket consultations for cultured animal cell foods. <4> On January 3, 2024, Blue Ridge Beef of Statesville, NC, expanded a voluntary recall to include additional lot numbers for its raw pet food products due to potential contamination with Salmonella and Listeria monocytogenes. The recall affects 2 lb logs of Kitten Grind (UPC 8 54298 00101 6), Kitten Mix (UPC 8 54298 00143 6), and Puppy Mix (UPC 8 54298 00169 6). The expansion covered all lots with 'used by' dates from N24 1114 to N24 1224. The action was taken after the North Carolina Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services notified the firm on December 15, 2023, that product samples had tested positive for the pathogens. The recall, which was an expansion of a previous one from December 22, 2023, now includes distribution to 16 states: Connecticut, Florida, Iowa, Illinois, Massachusetts, Maryland, Michigan, North Carolina, New York, Ohio, Oregon, Pennsylvania, Rhode Island, Tennessee, Virginia, and Wisconsin. No illnesses had been reported at the time of the announcement. Consumers were advised to destroy the product and contact the company for a refund. <5> Multiple food recalls were issued in late December 2023. On December 31, 2023, Valley Meats, LLC recalled raw ground beef because of potential E. coli O157:H7 contamination. [8] A day earlier, on December 30, 2023, Reckitt/Mead Johnson Nutrition recalled batches of Nutramigen Powder infant formula due to possible Cronobacter sakazakii contamination. [8, 10] On December 29, 2023, Ocean Group, Inc. initiated a recall for salmon due to Listeria monocytogenes. [8] Additionally, on December 28, 2023, Nam & Son of MD recalled one-pound bags of soybean sprouts because of potential contamination with Listeria monocytogenes; this was prompted by testing from the state of Virginia. These revised fees apply to basetime, overtime, holiday, and laboratory services for meat, poultry, and egg product establishments, in addition to importers and exporters. The new rates were scheduled to become effective on January 14, 2024. <7> The U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) and the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) have concluded their investigation into a multi-state Salmonella Thompson outbreak linked to recalled Gills Onions brand fresh diced onions. The illnesses began on dates ranging from August 2, 2023, to November 11, 2023. As part of the investigation, Gills Onions voluntarily recalled several fresh diced onion products on October 23, 2023. The recalled products are no longer for sale, and their use-by dates have passed. Investigators confirmed the outbreak strain in samples taken from the farm that supplied the onions. <8> Bix Produce Company of Little Canada, Minnesota, voluntarily recalled "Grab N' Go" containers of fresh-cut cantaloupe and mixed fruit cups under the brands Created Fresh! and Jack & Olive due to potential Salmonella contamination. The recalled products were distributed between October 19 and October 20, 2023, to convenience stores, delis, and business cafes in Minnesota, North Dakota, South Dakota, and Wisconsin. The affected items had "sell by" dates of October 25, 2023, and October 26, 2023, and were beyond their shelf-life when the recall was announced. No illnesses were reported in direct connection to the Bix Produce products. An earlier, separate recall on October 31, 2023, also involved Bix Produce for "Freshpoint Bix Produce Cantaloupe" distributed in Iowa, Minnesota, North Dakota, and Wisconsin. <9> In November 2023, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) began investigating a multi-state Salmonella outbreak linked to whole and pre-cut cantaloupes. The initial recalls from suppliers like Sofia Produce (doing business as TruFresh) began as early as November 9, 2023, and expanded to include additional producers and products containing cantaloupe throughout the month. The outbreak was caused by two Salmonella strains, Sundsvall and Oranienburg. Illnesses began on dates ranging from October 15, 2023, to December 25, 2023. By the time the outbreak was declared over on January 19, 2024, it had resulted in 407 reported illnesses across 44 states, leading to 158 hospitalizations and six deaths. The outbreak also affected Canada and was noted for its severity, particularly among children under five and adults over 65. <10> The HMC Group Marketing, Inc., doing business as HMC Farms, voluntarily recalled conventional peaches, plums, and nectarines on November 17, 2023, due to potential contamination with Listeria monocytogenes. The recall, announced via the FDA, applied to fruit sold nationwide between May 1, 2023, and November 15, 2023, as well as fruit sold during the same period in 2022. The recalled fruit was sold individually with PLU stickers or in 2-pound bags under the brand names "HMC Farms" and "Signature Farms". Retailers that sold the fruit included Walmart, Sam's Club, Publix, Sprouts Farmers Market, ALDI, and various stores under the Albertsons Company banner. The outbreak was declared over by the CDC as of January 30, 2024.

The recall was announced by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) on June 24, 2024. [3] The move came after FDA product sampling detected the presence of the bacteria. [3, 4] The recall encompasses 67 products across 13 brands, including well-known names like Friendly's, Hershey's, Jeni's, and ChipWich. [2] Other affected brands are Abilyn's Frozen Bakery, AMAFruits, Cumberland Farms, Dolcezza Gelato, LaSalle, Marco, Taharka Brothers, The Frozen Farmer, and Yelloh!. [4, 5] The recalled items, which include ice cream cakes, sandwiches, and sorbets, were distributed across the country through retail stores and direct delivery. [3, 7] In response to the findings, Totally Cool, Inc. has stopped all production and distribution of the implicated products and is conducting an ongoing investigation. [3, 4] Consumers are advised to return any recalled products to the place of purchase for a full refund. [3, 7] As of the announcement, no illnesses had been reported in connection with the recall. [3, 7] *Listeria monocytogenes* can cause serious and sometimes fatal infections, particularly in vulnerable populations such as young children, the elderly, and individuals with weakened immune systems. [3, 5] <2> Snapchill LLC of Green Bay, Wisconsin, voluntarily recalled all of its canned coffee products that are within their expiration date. [4] The recall was initiated because the company's current manufacturing process could potentially allow for the growth and production of Clostridium botulinum, a bacterium that produces a deadly neurotoxin causing botulism. [1, 4] The issue was identified after the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) notified Snapchill that the required low-acid canned foods process for manufacturing had not been filed with the agency. [1, 2, 4] The recall applies to a wide range of coffee products sold nationwide under approximately 128 different brand names, which can be identified by the language "Produced and distributed by Snapchill LLC" on the label. [1] At the time of the recall announcement, no illnesses had been reported, and Snapchill was not aware of any of its products containing the botulinum toxin. [2, 4, 6] Consumers were advised to either destroy the products or return them to the point of purchase for a refund. [1] Throughout 2023, the most common reasons for recalls also included undeclared milk, Listeria monocytogenes, and undeclared peanuts. [1] Notably, a significant Salmonella outbreak linked to cantaloupes led to numerous recalls from multiple brands in November 2023. The event, established by the World Health Organization (WHO) and the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO), aimed to raise awareness and inspire action to prevent foodborne diseases by emphasizing preparedness for food safety incidents. In the United States, various government bodies, including the FDA and USDA, participated in awareness-raising activities. Notable figures such as the FDA Deputy Commissioner for Human Foods and the USDA Deputy Under Secretary for Food Safety attended a related event at the Milken Institute School of Public Health in Washington, D.C. <5> In 2023, the first and third quarters had the lowest number of food recalls, while the second and fourth quarters saw the highest. The report specifically highlighted that in the third quarter, while overall recall events and units decreased from the second quarter, USDA-regulated recalls rose by 50%. The primary drivers for recalls were biological contaminants and undeclared allergens, which together accounted for 76% of all incidents. Recent related events (events are separated by numbered tags): <1> Albertsons Companies initiated and subsequently expanded a voluntary recall of select items containing tuna salad due to potential contamination with Listeria monocytogenes. The recall originated after a supplier, Reser's Fine Foods, issued its own recall for breadcrumbs used as an ingredient in the tuna salad, which were potentially contaminated. The initial recall on July 17, 2025, affected Albertsons, Randalls, and Tom Thumb stores in Arkansas, Louisiana, Oklahoma, and Texas. [1, 2, 3] The recall was later expanded on July 26, 2025, to include Jewel Osco stores in Illinois, Indiana, and Iowa. [4] The FDA published the first announcement of the recall on July 21, 2025. [1] <2> A multistate outbreak of Salmonella Anatum infections has been linked to recalled frozen sprouted beans produced by Chetak LLC Group under the brand name 'Deep'. As of July 17, 2025, 11 individuals have been reported sick across 10 states: Connecticut, Florida, Illinois, Massachusetts, Minnesota, New Jersey, Pennsylvania, Tennessee, Virginia, and Washington. The illnesses began on dates ranging from October 22, 2024, to June 24, 2025. Out of the 11 reported cases, four people have been hospitalized, but no deaths have been reported. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) are investigating the outbreak. The FDA found a match between the Salmonella strain in the product samples and the one causing the illnesses through routine product sampling in May 2025 and whole genome sequencing. In response, on July 16, 2025, Chetak LLC Group recalled Deep-brand frozen sprouted mat (moth) beans and frozen sprouted moong (mung) beans sold in 1 LB (454 g) packages with specific lot codes. <3> The 2025 annual Food Safety Summit was held from May 12 to 15 at the Donald E. Stephens Convention Center in Rosemont, Illinois. The four-day gathering brought together international professionals from the food service, retail, manufacturing, distribution, produce, regulatory, and academic sectors. The summit served as a platform to discuss the latest advancements, strategies, and best practices in food safety, with educational sessions covering timely issues such as sanitation, leveraging artificial intelligence, and allergen management. <4> LLK Trading Inc. of Linden, New Jersey, recalled its 200-gram packages of 'Needle Mushrooms,' also labeled as enoki mushrooms, due to potential contamination with Listeria monocytogenes. The risk was identified after routine testing by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) detected the pathogen in a sample. The recalled products, which come in a package with a clear plastic top and a non-transparent blue bottom, were distributed to Bally Produce Corp. in Maspeth, New York, and subsequently sold at Datang Supermarket Inc. Distribution of the mushrooms was suspended pending an investigation by the company and the FDA. As of the recall announcement, no illnesses had been reported. Consumers were urged not to consume the mushrooms and to return them to the place of purchase for a full refund. <5> An outbreak of Salmonella Enteritidis infections linked to eggs from August Egg Company of Hilmar, California, has been declared over by the CDC, and the FDA has concluded its investigation. [1, 5, 7] The outbreak resulted in 134 confirmed cases across 10 states, leading to 38 hospitalizations and one reported death. [1, 2, 5] Illnesses began on dates ranging from February 24, 2025, to June 6, 2025. [2, 5] The investigation, a collaboration between the CDC, FDA, and state officials, traced the source to brown cage-free and certified organic eggs. [1, 2] In response, August Egg Company issued a recall on June 6, 2025, for the affected eggs which were distributed to various retailers. [6, 9, 10] <6> The U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), along with state public health officials, are investigating multistate outbreaks of Salmonella Enteritidis, Indiana, London, and Mbandaka infections. Epidemiologic, traceback, and laboratory data have linked these outbreaks to contact with backyard poultry. As of June 23, 2025, 187 infected individuals have been reported across 42 states, with illness onset dates ranging from February 9, 2025, to May 31, 2025. Based on data from 138 of the patients, 42 people (30%) have been hospitalized, and one death has been reported from Illinois. <7> The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA), Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), and the USDA's Food Safety and Inspection Service (FSIS) are jointly investigating a multi-state outbreak of Listeria monocytogenes. [1] The investigation has linked the infections to pre-made chicken fettuccine alfredo meals produced by FreshRealm, Inc. at its facilities in San Clemente, California; Montezuma, Georgia; and Indianapolis, Indiana. [2, 3] On June 17, 2025, FreshRealm, Inc. voluntarily recalled all implicated products produced prior to that date. [1, 3] The recalled ready-to-eat meals were distributed nationwide to major retailers, including Walmart under the "Marketside" brand and Kroger under the "Home Chef" brand. [2, 4, 5] As of the public announcement on June 18, 2025, the outbreak included 17 reported cases across 13 states, with illnesses starting between July 2024 and May 2025. [1, 2] The outbreak has resulted in severe outcomes, including 16 hospitalizations, three deaths, and one fetal loss. [1, 2, 3] <8> On June 18, 2025, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) announced and opened a public comment period for its proposed "Post-market Assessment Prioritization Tool." This new method is intended to provide a transparent, systematic, and science-based approach to rank and prioritize which chemicals in the food supply require post-market assessment. The tool will assign a score to chemicals based on public health criteria, such as toxicity, and other factors, like stakeholder concern, to help the FDA allocate resources more efficiently to chemicals that may pose the greatest public health risk. Initially, the deadline for public comment was set for July 18, 2025. However, in response to requests from various stakeholders, the FDA announced on July 14, 2025, that it was extending the comment period by 30 days. The final, extended deadline for submitting comments is now August 18, 2025. <9> In June 2025, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) issued warning letters to Zest US Wholesale Inc. of Anaheim, CA, and Xin Ao International Group Corp. of Staten Island, NY, for significant violations of the Foreign Supplier Verification Program (FSVP). [3] The warning letter to Zest US Wholesale was issued on June 3, 2025, following an inspection on April 28, 2025. The company failed to develop, maintain, or follow an FSVP for imported products such as milk chocolate bars, pistachio spread, and coconut almond truffles. [3] The FDA also noted that Zest US Wholesale had not fulfilled food facility registration requirements. [4] The warning letter to Xin Ao International Group Corp. was issued on June 6, 2025. [2] This followed an FSVP inspection from April 23 to May 6, 2025, which found the company had not developed an FSVP for imported seafood and enoki mushrooms. [2, 3] An earlier inspection of Xin Ao had also been conducted in May 2023. [2] For both companies, the FDA issued a Form 483a outlining the violations and warned that continued noncompliance could lead to the detention of their imported products without physical examination. [2, 3]
